title: Erdős #902: Tournament Domination
description: Let f(n) be minimal such that there is a tournament on f(n) vertices such that every set of n vertices is dominated. Known: f(1)=3, f(2)=7, f(3)=19. Bounds: n·2^n ≪ f(n) ≪ n²·2^n.

meta.author: Paul Erdős, György Szekeres, Esther Szekeres
meta.assumptions: 23 axioms: exists_n_dominating, f_is_minimum, f_1, and 20 more. See Lean source for complete statements.

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős posed this question about tournament domination in 1963, as part of his deep investigation into extremal combinatorics. A tournament is a complete directed graph — every pair of vertices has exactly one directed edge (one player beats the other). The function $f(n)$ gives the minimum tournament size where every $n$-element set of vertices is dominated by some external vertex: there exists a vertex $v$ not in the set that beats every member.

Szekeres and Szekeres (1965) established the lower bound $f(n) \geq n \cdot 2^n$ using an elegant counting argument: each vertex dominates at most $\binom{N-1}{n}$ of the $\binom{N}{n}$ possible $n$-sets, and the total number of dominated $n$-sets must be at least $\binom{N}{n}$, requiring $N$ to be large. The probabilistic method, pioneered by Erdős, gives the upper bound $f(n) \leq C \cdot n^2 \cdot 2^n$: a random tournament of this size satisfies the domination property with positive probability.

Only $f(1) = 3$ (the cyclic tournament, "Rock-Paper-Scissors"), $f(2) = 7$ (the Paley tournament on $\mathbb{F}_7$, constructed via quadratic residues), and $f(3) = 19$ (found by computer search) are known exactly. Tournament domination connects to the theory of voting paradoxes (Condorcet, 1785): the domination property means that for any committee of $n$ candidates, there exists an outsider who defeats every committee member in pairwise comparison — a quantitative strengthening of Condorcet's paradox. The algebraic structure of Paley tournaments, constructed from the Legendre symbol $(a/p)$, provides the best known explicit constructions, linking the problem to quadratic residues and number theory.
overview.problemStatement: Let f(n) be minimal such that there is a tournament on f(n) vertices such that every set of n vertices is dominated by at least one other vertex. Estimate f(n).
overview.text: Let f(n) be minimal such that there is a tournament on f(n) vertices such that every set of n vertices is dominated. Known: f(1)=3, f(2)=7, f(3)=19. Bounds: n·2^n ≪ f(n) ≪ n²·2^n.
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize the tournament and domination definitions, the function f(n), known values f(1), f(2), f(3), Szekeres lower bound, Erdős upper bound, asymptotic behavior, Paley tournaments, quadratic residues, the probabilistic method, and connections to coding theory.

sections.title: Tournament Definitions
sections.mathContext: Tournament: complete directed graph (every pair has exactly one directed edge). Order = number of vertices.

sections.title: Domination
sections.mathContext: Vertex $v$ dominates $u$ if $v \\to u$. Set $S$ is dominated by $v$ if $v$ dominates every $u \\in S$. $n$-dominating: every $n$-subset is dominated by some vertex.

sections.title: The Function f(n)
sections.summary: Definition of f(n) as minimal n-dominating tournament order
sections.mathContext: $f(n)$ = minimum number of vertices in an $n$-dominating tournament. Equivalently: smallest tournament where every $n$-element subset has a common dominator.

sections.title: Lower Bound
sections.mathContext: Szekeres-Szekeres (1965): $f(n) \\geq c \\cdot n \\cdot 2^n$. Counting argument: each vertex dominates $\\sim$ half the others, so covering all $n$-subsets requires $\\Omega(n \\cdot 2^n)$ vertices.

sections.title: Upper Bound
sections.mathContext: Erdos (1963): $f(n) \\leq C \\cdot n^2 \\cdot 2^n$. Probabilistic: a random tournament of this size is $n$-dominating with positive probability.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures Erdős Problem #902 on tournament domination. The function f(n) gives the minimum tournament size where every n-set is dominated. Known values are f(1)=3, f(2)=7, f(3)=19, with bounds n·2^n ≪ f(n) ≪ n²·2^n.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: The gap between the bounds suggests deep structure in extremal tournaments.

Paley tournaments provide optimal constructions for certain orders. The problem connects to covering codes and the probabilistic method.
openQuestions: What is the exact asymptotic growth of f(n)? Is f(n) = Θ(n·2^n) or Θ(n²·2^n)?
Can the upper bound be improved to f(n) ≪ n·2^n, matching the Szekeres lower bound?
What is f(4)? The next unknown value likely lies in the range [49, 200].
Are Paley tournaments asymptotically optimal for the domination property?
Can algebraic or spectral methods (beyond Paley constructions) yield explicit n-dominating tournaments matching the probabilistic bound?

references.title: Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory
references.note: Contains the formulation of Problem 902 on tournament domination, alongside the Erdős–Graham collection of open problems in combinatorics and number theory.

references.title: On a problem of Schütte and Erdős
references.note: Established the lower bound f(n) ≥ n·2ⁿ for the tournament domination function. The counting argument — bounding how many n-sets each vertex can dominate — is the basis of the axiomatic lower bound in this formalization.

references.authors: Graham, Ronald L.; Spencer, Joel H.
references.title: A constructive solution to a tournament problem
references.note: Uses Paley tournaments (constructed from quadratic residues mod p) to give explicit dominating tournaments, providing constructive upper bounds for f(n). The Paley construction is formalized in this entry.

references.title: The Probabilistic Method
references.note: Standard reference for the probabilistic method in combinatorics. Chapter 3 covers tournaments and includes the probabilistic upper bound f(n) ≤ O(n²·2ⁿ) that complements the Szekeres lower bound.

references.title: Topics on Tournaments
references.note: Foundational monograph on tournament theory, covering scoring sequences, Hamiltonian paths, and domination — the structural background for Problem 902.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #901 (Property B for hypergraphs) shares the same asymptotic structure: m(n) lies between c·n·2^n and C·n²·2^n, with the same factor-of-n gap. Both problems use the probabilistic method for the upper bound and counting/double-counting for the lower bound. The Erdős–Lovász conjecture m(n) = Θ(n·2^n) parallels the conjecture f(n) = Θ(n·2^n) here.
Both involve partition or extremal combinatorics — studying when combinatorial structures must contain specific subconfigurations.

Erdős #165 on R(3,k) — the Ramsey number for triangle-free graphs — uses the probabilistic method and the Lovász Local Lemma to establish asymptotic bounds, the same core technique that gives the upper bound f(n) ≤ O(n²·2^n) in tournament domination. Both problems exemplify how probabilistic existence proofs yield the best known upper bounds in extremal combinatorics.

The Erdős–Szekeres theorem on monotone subsequences was proved by the same George and Esther Szekeres who established the lower bound f(n) ≥ c·n·2^n for tournament domination. Both results involve extremal combinatorial configurations on ordered or directed structures, and both use elegant counting arguments (pigeonhole for Erdős–Szekeres, double counting for the domination lower bound).

Quadratic reciprocity and the Legendre symbol underpin the Paley tournament construction central to Problem #902. The Paley tournament on a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) directs edge a → b iff (b−a)/p = 1 (a quadratic residue). The fact that exactly (p−1)/2 nonzero elements are quadratic residues — a consequence of the theory formalized in quadratic reciprocity — gives Paley tournaments their symmetric structure and optimal domination properties.

Ramsey's theorem guarantees monochromatic cliques in edge-colored complete graphs. Tournament domination is a directed analogue: instead of finding monochromatic structure, one seeks a vertex that dominates an entire subset. Both problems live in the extremal combinatorics of complete graphs, and the probabilistic method (pioneered by Erdős) gives the best bounds for both. The exponential growth 2^n appears in both Ramsey numbers and the domination function f(n).

The Friendship Theorem (Erdős–Rényi–Sós) proves that if every pair of vertices in a finite graph shares exactly one common neighbor, then a universal vertex exists — a structural result about domination in undirected graphs. Tournament domination generalizes this theme to directed graphs: instead of a single universal vertex, one seeks a vertex that out-dominates an entire n-element subset. Both results reveal how local constraints force global structure.

Erdős #900 on longest paths in sparse random graphs G(n, cn) uses the probabilistic method to show phase transitions in random graph structure. The upper bound for tournament domination similarly analyzes random tournaments: a random tournament on O(n²·2^n) vertices is n-dominating with positive probability. Both problems illustrate how random combinatorial objects achieve extremal properties that are hard to construct explicitly.
